summary:
East Kalimantan stands under Indonesia's national framework, which applies in full to visitors in the province. Private same-sex conduct is not itself criminalised under national law, but it carries no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection, and legal gender change is conditional on sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval.

The amended penal code, passed in December 2022 and in force from 2 January 2026, penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to one year's imprisonment on complaint. Same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, so the provision reaches all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

No incident documentation was found for East Kalimantan itself. An international human-rights analysis lists the province among eight provinces carrying discriminatory provincial regulations, where province, district and city rules overlap national law, but no deviation from the national position was material enough to score separately.

Official policy frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture among nonmilitary threats alongside terrorism and drug addiction. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing to a wave of vigilante attacks: in July 2026 mobs attacked trans women in several cities, with no prosecutions reported, and commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman; Amnesty International stated that the gathering violated no law and called the operation a blatant violation of human rights and privacy.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveller in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022 and died in custody. His mother alleges that police beat him and that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release; Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.
tangentialFactors:
Two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women alongside national morality provisions. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025; those punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors. East Kalimantan is not among them.

Indonesia voted against the UN independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025, an official position consistent with the October 2025 decree's treatment of LGBTQ+ promotion as a threat.

Public opinion data indicates the social environment a trans visitor enters. Pew reported in 2025 that 93% of Indonesians view homosexuality as morally unacceptable, and estimated 95% opposition to same-sex marriage in 2023. Civil society describes conditions as rapidly worsening.

Subnational regulation varies across Indonesia, which is the pattern the discriminatory-regulation listing for East Kalimantan sits within. A 2021 Bogor city bylaw and a 2020 raid in which a gay transgender couple was released for lack of a regional regulation both show that district rules diverge from one another and from national law.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change for residents of East Kalimantan requires sex-reassignment surgery and judicial approval; there is no administrative route that avoids the courts.

Residents have no anti-discrimination protection and no hate-crime enhancement based on gender identity or sexual orientation, in employment, housing, or public services.

Residents face the extra-marital sex provision of the amended penal code on the same terms as visitors, with prosecution on complaint and penalties of up to one year's imprisonment.

Trans women in Indonesia were attacked by mobs in several cities in July 2026 with no prosecutions reported, and the October 2025 presidential decree places the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture within national threat monitoring.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents any incident, arrest, raid, or provincial regulation specific to East Kalimantan. The province's assessment rests on the national framework plus a listing in an international human-rights analysis of provinces with discriminatory subnational regulations; the underlying analysis itself was not re-examined here.

Sources differ on the penalty for extra-marital sex under the amended penal code: the national profile records up to two years' imprisonment, while the encyclopaedic source used here records up to one year on complaint. The discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether East Kalimantan has enacted its own district or city bylaws on morality, gender expression, or LGBTQ+ conduct is not sourced, and neither is any enforcement practice by the provincial police distinct from national practice.

The claim that prosecutions of same-sex relations are selective rather than systematic rests on reporting rather than case-level data for this province.
